673.title: The winter solstice
673.hook: the longest night, and the light returns from here
673.howItsDone: Several traditions hold festivals of light around the winter solstice, each with its own meaning; some people mark the longest night simply by lighting a candle and keeping company.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Saturnalia, when masters served and Seneca kept a sober head. Your line was roles reversed. Who did you give something to? Day six hundred seventy-three.

Four-thirty in the afternoon and it's already dark. You leave work in the dark; you might have arrived in it too. In the far north, the sun barely clears the horizon, or doesn't rise at all. And yet, all around the world, this darkest stretch of the year is full of lights. Strings of them on houses. Candles in windows. In Iran, families stay up through Yalda, the longest night, eating pomegranates and reading poetry. Other traditions keep their own festivals of light around now, each with its own meaning. Today on the porch: the winter solstice.
screen: `DARK AT FOUR-THIRTY.` → `CANDLES IN WINDOWS.` → `THE LONGEST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the turn at the bottom. Back at the summer solstice, we saw that the peak of the light was also the start of its going. Now it's the mirror: the longest night is the moment the light starts coming back. Tomorrow will be a little longer than today. Nobody will notice, at first. Second, Seneca on the seasons. In one of his letters, he tells Lucilius that the world itself runs on change. Winter brings the cold, and we have to shiver. Summer brings the heat, and we have to sweat. We can't change that order, he says, but we can take on a great spirit, worthy of a good person, and bear what comes bravely, in agreement with nature. The dark isn't a punishment. It's part of the turning. Third, a Stoic and his lamp. Epictetus tells his students that he once had an iron lamp by his household gods, and a thief stole it. His response: tomorrow, I'll buy a clay one. And the thief, Epictetus says, paid a higher price: to get the lamp, he agreed to become a thief. A lamp, for Epictetus, can be replaced. What he chooses to be cannot be stolen. Fourth, why a candle. A candle in the dark doesn't argue with the night. It doesn't make it day. It just makes a small circle where you can see a face, a page, your own hands. That's often what getting through a hard season looks like: not ending the dark, but keeping one small light going until the days lengthen on their own.
screen: `THE LONGEST NIGHT IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `WINTER BRINGS COLD: WE SHIVER.` · `EPICTETUS'S STOLEN LAMP.` · `A SMALL CIRCLE OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT RETURNS.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, safely, somewhere you can watch it. If not, turn on one small lamp and turn the others off. Look at the flame or the glow. Notice how far the light reaches, and where the dark begins. Don't try to push the dark away. Let the small light be enough. Think of one person who's in a dark season right now. Hold them in mind in this small circle of light. The bell holds the time.
The winter solstice: the longest night of the year, and the turning point after which the light returns, little by little. Today's word.
Your line: the light returns. Light one small light tonight, a candle or a lamp, and if someone you love is in the dark, send them a few words. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: A Stoic birthday
674.hook: Seneca would ask: how much of this past year did you really live?
674.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca use a birthday or new year to review how much of the past year they truly lived, and what they want more of in the next.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the winter solstice, the longest night, and a small light kept going. Your line was the light returns. Did you light one, for yourself or someone else? Day six hundred seventy-four.

Candles on a cake. Someone counts them, or gives up and uses a number-shaped candle instead. Thirty-four. Fifty-two. Seventy-one. Everyone sings, slightly off key, and somebody says: another year older! The number is the headline of a birthday. It's the thing the cake, the card, the social media post all agree on. But Seneca, who wrote a whole essay about how we spend our time, would lean across the table, very politely, and ask a different question. Not how many years. How much of this past year did you actually live?
screen: `CANDLES ON A CAKE.` → `ANOTHER YEAR OLDER!` → `HOW MUCH DID YOU LIVE?`

segments.voice: First, the essay. Seneca's On the Shortness of Life, written to a friend named Paulinus, opens with a complaint everyone makes: life is too short. Seneca disagrees. Life is long enough, he says, if we use it well. It's we who make it short, by wasting it. Second, the audit. He asks the reader to imagine an old man and add up his years honestly. How many went to a demanding boss, to quarrels, to errands around the city, to worries he invented, to things he didn't even enjoy? Take those away, Seneca says, and you'll find he has far fewer years than he counts. Third, the sharpest line. You shouldn't think someone has lived long because of gray hair and wrinkles, he writes. That person hasn't lived long; they've been around long. It's like a sailor caught in a storm the moment he leaves the harbor, blown in circles for days. He didn't have a long voyage. He was just tossed about a lot. Fourth, a birthday on the porch. Seneca isn't asking for guilt. He's asking for an honest count. Which days this past year were actually lived, with attention, with people, with something that mattered? Those count. The others aren't failures; they're information. And a birthday is a good day to ask, because the next year hasn't been spent yet. Seneca's own phrase for the difference: one person has lived long, another has only been around long. A birthday is a chance to move a few days from the second column to the first.
screen: `LIFE IS LONG, IF YOU USE IT.` · `SUBTRACT THE WASTED YEARS.` · `NOT LIVED LONG: AROUND LONG.` · `AN HONEST COUNT, NOT GUILT.` · then, large: `HOW MUCH DID I LIVE?`

segments.voice: Whether it's your birthday or not, look back over the last twelve months. Find three days, or moments, when you were fully alive: present, awake, with people or work or a place that mattered. Picture each one clearly. Let them count. Then, gently, notice one stretch that slipped away, scrolling, worrying, rushing. No blame. Just ask: what would I want more of, and less of, in the year ahead? The bell holds the time.
A Stoic birthday: counting not the years but the life in them, with Seneca's honest question, how much of this year did I really live? Today's word.
Your line: how much did I live. Make one hour today one of the lived ones: phone away, fully there for whatever you're doing. Day six hundred seventy-four.

675.title: The Stoic morning
675.hook: preview, one principle, and a clear intention
675.howItsDone: Some modern Stoic practitioners begin the day with a short routine drawn from Marcus and Epictetus: previewing difficulties, recalling one principle, and setting an intention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Stoic birthday, and Seneca's honest count. Your line was how much did I live. Was there one fully lived hour? Day six hundred seventy-five.

The alarm goes off, and the phone is already in reach. Before feet touch the floor, a thumb is scrolling: messages, headlines, someone's vacation, a work email marked urgent. A minute or two in, the day's mood has been set by whoever got there first. The turning year is behind us now. For the next stretch of the porch, we're putting a year of Stoic reading to work in ordinary life: morning, evening, work, home, the hard days and the good ones. And it starts where every day starts. Today: the Stoic morning.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE PHONE, THE HEADLINES.` → `DECIDED BY WHOEVER GOT THERE FIRST.` → `LIVING THE PORCH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Three parts, gathered from a year of reading, mostly from Marcus. First, preview. Marcus opens book two of his notebook with this, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds grim. But read on, and he says none of them can really harm him, and that they're his kin, made for working together. The preview isn't pessimism. It's packing an umbrella: when the rude email comes, you've already met it once, calmly, in your head. Second, one principle. Marcus tells himself to keep his principles ready the way a doctor keeps instruments close at hand for sudden cases. Not a whole philosophy. One line for the day. Maybe Epictetus's split: some things are up to me, some aren't. Maybe Seneca's: begin now. Maybe one you've written yourself this year. Third, intention. On a morning when Marcus didn't want to get up, and he admits to those, he asks himself what he was made for: to lie under the blankets keeping warm, or to do the work of a human being? An intention answers that for today. Not a to-do list. A how: patient with my kids, honest in the meeting, kind on the phone. Fourth, the whole thing takes about two minutes. Preview, principle, intention. Before the phone, if you can. The day will still surprise you. But you'll meet it as yourself, rather than as whoever the first notification decided you'd be.
screen: `PREVIEW: MEET THE DAY ONCE, CALMLY.` · `ONE PRINCIPLE, READY AT HAND.` · `INTENTION: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.` · `TWO MINUTES, BEFORE THE PHONE.` · then, large: `PREVIEW, PRINCIPLE, INTENTION.`

segments.voice: Let's do a Stoic morning now, whatever time it is. Preview: picture the rest of your day. Where's the likely friction, a person, a task, a delay? Meet it once in your mind, calmly. Principle: choose one line to carry, from this year or your own. Say it silently. Intention: finish this sentence for yourself, today I want to be someone who. Then sit with all three, and let them settle. The bell holds the time.
The Stoic morning: a two-minute start, preview the day, choose one principle, set a clear intention, before the world decides for you. Today's word.
Your line: preview, principle, intention. Tomorrow morning, before you touch your phone, give those three their two minutes. Day six hundred seventy-five.

676.title: The Stoic evening
676.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners end the day with a short review modeled on Seneca and Sextius: what went well, where they slipped, how they grew, followed by self-forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Stoic morning. Your line was preview, principle, intention. Did you get your two minutes before the phone? Today, the other end of the day. Day six hundred seventy-six.

Lights out. The head hits the pillow, and the replay starts on its own. The thing you said in the meeting. The text you didn't answer. The way you snapped at your partner over the dishes. Round and round, the loop that keeps people awake. Seneca had a different way of ending the day. It took a few minutes, it happened on purpose, and it ended with something like a pardon. He borrowed it from an older philosopher, and he described it in his essay On Anger. Today: the Stoic evening.
screen: `LIGHTS OUT, THE REPLAY STARTS.` → `THE LOOP THAT KEEPS YOU UP.` → `A REVIEW ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, where Seneca got it. He tells us that the philosopher Sextius, at the end of each day, before sleep, would question his own mind. Three questions. What bad habit have you healed today? What fault have you resisted? In what way are you better? Second, the habit's older roots. The Pythagoreans, earlier still, had verses that asked something similar each night: where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone? Epictetus quotes those lines to his students. In Greek the first question is pē parebēn: where did I step aside? Third, how Seneca does it. When the lamp is out, he says, and his wife, who knows his habit, has gone quiet, he goes over his whole day, every word and deed. He hides nothing from himself and skips nothing. Then he gives an example. In that argument, you spoke too sharply. Don't argue with people who can't be taught. And the verdict? See that you don't do it again, he tells himself. This time, I forgive you. Fourth, why gently matters. The bedtime replay and the Stoic review look alike, but they work in opposite directions. The replay is a loop: same scene, more anxiety, no ending. The review is a line: look, learn one thing, forgive, close the file. Seneca says sleep after it is especially sweet, because the mind has been praised or warned and knows where it stands. Three questions, honest and kind, and then you can let the day go.
screen: `SEXTIUS'S THREE QUESTIONS.` · `PĒ PAREBĒN: WHERE DID I GO WRONG?` · `THIS TIME, I FORGIVE YOU.` · `A LINE, NOT A LOOP.` · then, large: `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Do a short evening review now, wherever you are in the day. First: what habit did you resist, even a little, today? Second: where did you slip? Name one moment plainly, without arguing for yourself or against yourself. Third: in what way were you better, even slightly? Let one honest answer come to each. Then, if it helps, say Seneca's verdict silently: don't do it again; this time, I forgive you. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The Stoic evening: Seneca's nightly review, three honest questions about the day, and then a gentle pardon so you can sleep. Today's word.
Your line: three questions. Tonight, with the lights out, ask them, answer once, forgive once, and then let the day go. Day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: Stoic at work
677.hook: duties, roles, and control at work
677.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners sort work worries into what is and isn't up to them, then give full effort to their own part and the duties of their role.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Stoic evening, Sextius's questions and Seneca's pardon. Your line was three questions. Did you ask them in the dark, and let the day go? Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Sunday night, around eight. The feeling arrives on schedule: the project that's behind, the manager who's hard to read, the rumor about layoffs, the colleague who takes credit. Some of it is real work. Some of it is weather. All of it lands in the same knot in your stomach. The Stoics didn't have open-plan offices or quarterly reviews. But many of Epictetus's students were young men headed for posts in public life, and Marcus wrote his notebook while hearing cases and running campaigns. They had a lot to say about doing work without letting it own you. Today: Stoic at work.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, EIGHT O'CLOCK.` → `REAL WORK, AND WEATHER.` → `ONE KNOT IN THE STOMACH.`

segments.voice: First, the split. The Handbook opens with it: some things are up to us, and some are not. At work, that sorts quickly. Up to you: how carefully you do the task, how honestly you speak, how you treat the people around you, whether you ask for help. Not up to you: the budget, the reorganization, whether your manager likes your idea, the economy. Second, roles. We met this idea with Cicero a month ago; Epictetus puts it in one line: our duties are measured by our relationships. You are a colleague, so act as a good colleague. You are someone's manager, or someone's report, so ask what that role asks of you, today, at this desk. Third, the Stoic word for this. Kathēkon: an appropriate action, the fitting thing for someone in your place to do. It isn't heroic. It's the email answered clearly, the meeting attended fully, the mistake owned up to. Fourth, putting them together. A lot of work worry comes from mixing the two columns, carrying the layoff rumor as if it were your task, or treating your own sloppy report as if it were fate. When you sort them, the knot loosens a little. The first column gets your full effort. The second gets your attention, maybe your preparation, but not your sleep. Marcus, in the middle of his own work, reminded himself more than once to do the thing in front of him with simple dignity, as if it were the last thing he would ever do.
screen: `UP TO ME, NOT UP TO ME.` · `DUTIES MEASURED BY ROLES.` · `KATHĒKON: THE FITTING THING.` · `TWO COLUMNS, ONE KNOT LOOSENED.` · then, large: `MY PART AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring one work worry to mind. If you're not working right now, choose a worry from school, volunteering or caregiving. Picture a page with two columns. In the left, up to me: what you can actually do about it. Write those in your mind, one by one. In the right, not up to me: what you can't control. Put those there, and let them stay there. Now look at the left column only. Pick one thing from it to do. The bell holds the time.
Stoic at work: doing your role's fitting part fully, and leaving what isn't up to you in its own column. Today's word.
Your line: my part at work. Do the one thing from your left column today, and when the right column whispers, tell it where it belongs. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Stoic at home
678.hook: the hive, the household, the people you live with
678.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat the household as the first circle of their care, doing small unasked tasks for the people they live with without keeping score.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic at work, two columns and the fitting thing. Your line was my part at work. Did you do the one thing from the left column? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

The sink has a pan in it that's been soaking since Tuesday. Nobody remembers whose it is. It's become a sort of household monument. Everyone walks past it. Everyone has an opinion about it. Nobody touches it. If you've lived with other people, roommates, a partner, kids, parents, you know this pan, or its cousin, the empty toilet paper roll. It's funny how hard it can be to be patient and good in the place where we're most ourselves. The Stoics thought home was exactly where philosophy gets tested. Today: Stoic at home.
screen: `THE PAN SOAKING SINCE TUESDAY.` → `EVERYONE WALKS PAST IT.` → `WHERE PHILOSOPHY GETS TESTED.`

segments.voice: First, the hive. Marcus Aurelius writes, in George Long's 1862 translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." One line, and a whole picture. A bee doesn't thrive by doing well while the hive falls apart. Whatever helps only me, at the expense of the people I live with, isn't really good for me either. Second, the circles. A later Stoic named Hierocles drew a picture of it. Imagine yourself at the center of a set of circles. The first ring is your own mind and body. The next is your closest family, then your wider family, neighbors, your town, and finally all of humanity. The task, he says, is to draw the circles inward: to treat the people in each ring a little more like the ones closer in. And the household is the very first ring past your own skin. Third, the Stoic word underneath. Oikeiōsis: making something your own, belonging. It comes from oikos, the Greek word for household. For the Stoics, care starts with what is closest and grows outward from there. Home isn't a break from virtue. It's the first ring it has to cross. Fourth, the pan. In practice, a Stoic at home isn't someone who never gets annoyed. It's someone who asks, what's good for the hive? And then does one small thing for it without keeping score. Wash the pan. Replace the roll. Not as a martyr, not as a point being made. Just as a bee who knows where it lives.
screen: `NOT GOOD FOR THE SWARM, NOR THE BEE.` · `HIEROCLES' CIRCLES, DRAWN INWARD.` · `OIKEIŌSIS: FROM OIKOS, HOUSEHOLD.` · `ONE THING FOR THE HIVE, NO SCORE.` · then, large: `FOR THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Picture your home and the people in it, or if you live alone, the people closest to you. See each face. Now picture the circles: you in the middle, then them. Notice whether there's any score being kept, about chores, about who gives more. Just notice; no blame. Then choose one small thing you could do for the house today, something nobody asked for. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without announcing it. The bell holds the time.
Stoic at home: treating the household as the hive and the first circle, and doing your part for it without keeping score. Today's word.
Your line: for the house. Do the one small thing you chose, and don't mention it. Let the house just be a little better. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: Stoic in grief
679.hook: honest grief, the seasons, sweet memory
679.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca treat grief as something to feel honestly rather than suppress, and over time to turn into grateful memory of the person lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic at home, the bee and the hive. Your line was for the house. Did the one quiet thing get done, without a word about it? Day six hundred seventy-nine, the end of a week.

Someone at the funeral says it to the dead man's daughter, meaning well: you're being so strong. She hasn't cried in front of anyone. She went back to work on Monday. People admire it. And at two in the morning, alone in her kitchen, it isn't strength at all. It's a held breath. That's the common picture of Stoic grief: a stiff upper lip, nothing shown. Earlier this year we read Seneca admitting he'd wept too much for a friend. Today we gather what the porch says about grief into something to live by.
screen: `YOU'RE BEING SO STRONG.` → `TWO A.M., A HELD BREATH.` → `WHAT SENECA'S GRIEF LOOKS LIKE.`

segments.voice: Three threads from the year, held together. First, honest grief. Seneca, writing to Lucilius after a friend's death, doesn't tell him not to cry. He says the eyes shouldn't be dry when a friend is lost, nor should they overflow; tears are allowed, wailing isn't required. Then he confesses that when his own friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept beyond all measure, and he counts himself among those whom grief defeated. A teacher who admits that is not asking for stone. Second, the seasons. The Stoics placed death inside nature's turning, as we saw with the ripe olive. That isn't a way to cancel sorrow. It's a frame big enough to hold it. Leaves fall; we still miss the green. Seneca, writing to a mother three years into mourning her son, is gentle and patient, and also asks her, slowly, to let her life go on. Third, sweet memory. Seneca passes on a saying from his teacher Attalus: remembering lost friends can be pleasant, the way some fruits are good because they're a little sharp, or the way a very old wine has a bitterness that pleases. Seneca's own hope is that the memory of those we've lost becomes a joy rather than only a wound. Fourth, putting it together. Grief, in Seneca's letters, is honest grief: tears when they come, a loss held inside the turning year, and, over time, the person coming back as a memory that can be visited with something like gladness. Not instead of sorrow. Alongside it. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: the light returns. How much did I live. Preview, principle, intention. Three questions. My part at work. For the house. Grief, honestly. A week of carrying the porch into ordinary days.

Stoic in grief: honest tears, a loss held within nature's seasons, and a memory that slowly turns sweet. Not a stiff upper lip. Today's word.
